sixtySeconds.whatItDoes: scikit-learn is the standard Python library for classic machine learning. It provides dozens of ready-made algorithms for classification, regression and clustering, plus tools for preprocessing data, building pipelines, choosing models and evaluating them, all with one consistent fit and predict API.
sixtySeconds.problem: Implementing and comparing machine learning algorithms from scratch is slow and error-prone. scikit-learn gives you well-tested estimators and utilities that work the same way, so you can try models quickly on tabular data.
whoFor: Data scientists working with tabular data
sixtySeconds.whyChoose: Choose it for classic machine learning on structured data with excellent documentation. For deep learning, use a framework like PyTorch or Keras instead.

overview: scikit-learn is built on SciPy and distributed under the BSD 3-Clause license. It started in 2007 as a Google Summer of Code project by David Cournapeau and is maintained by a community of volunteers with support from several organisations.

Every model is an estimator with a fit method; after fitting you call predict on new data. Preprocessors and transformers such as StandardScaler share the same API but use transform, and they can be chained with a final predictor in a pipeline. The library also covers model selection and evaluation.

Install it with pip or conda once NumPy and SciPy are available. Plotting functions need Matplotlib, and some examples need pandas, seaborn, scikit-image or Plotly. Full documentation, a FAQ and a map for choosing the right model are on scikit-learn.org.
limitations: Not for deep learning or GPUs
Best suited to data that fits in memory

tutorial.title: Fit and predict with your first estimator
tutorial.useCase: Train a random forest on tiny example data, following the getting started guide.

steps.title: Fit a classifier
steps.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
clf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0)
X = [[ 1,  2,  3],
     [11, 12, 13]]
y = [0, 1]
clf.fit(X, y)

steps.title: Try a preprocessor
steps.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
X = [[0, 15],
     [1, -10]]
StandardScaler().fit(X).transform(X)

tutorial.expected: The guide shows the prediction returning array([0, 1]) and the scaler returning standardised values.
